attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: An unhedged present-tense observation. The normalised version keeps both parts: LLMs still hallucinate and still make boneheaded errors.

contract.note: Plain reading is ordinary and fair: frontier models still hallucinate at measurable rates and still fail some simple tasks. It does not strain for or against the speaker.

evidence.note: Independent Vectara benchmark, Nov 2025. Several frontier thinking models hallucinate in over 10% of summaries. Covers summarisation only, but that is enough to show measurable rates.
Same benchmark. Gemini-3-pro, then newly released, hallucinated in 13.6% of summaries.
Feb 2026 survey says significant reasoning failures persist even in seemingly simple scenarios. This matches 'boneheaded errors'.

reviews.rationale: Independent measurements from Nov 2025 show frontier models with hallucination rates above 10%. A Feb 2026 survey documents reasoning failures on simple tasks. Nothing in the packet shows either problem was eliminated. Both parts of the observation hold on the plain reading.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: A qualitative observation that reasoning remains a core unsolved problem for LLMs. 'Unsolved' fairly captures 'still one of the core issues'.

contract.note: The plain reading (reasoning failures remain a major recognised limitation, not a solved problem) is ordinary. The contract rightly notes that real progress can coexist with reasoning being a core issue.

evidence.note: Feb 2026 survey: significant reasoning failures persist in LLMs.
ARC Prize, Dec 2025: reasoning systems still have many flaws, and new ideas are needed.
Records major 2025 reasoning gains (IMO, ICPC, ARC-AGI-2). This tempers the claim but does not show reasoning was solved.

reviews.rationale: A Feb 2026 research survey and a Dec 2025 benchmark organisation both name reasoning flaws as a major remaining limitation. The progress noted in e3 does not meet the contradiction condition, since it does not show reasoning had become solved or minor.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion. The promises are attributed to others, but the claim that such promises keep being made is his.

semantics.note: An observation that AGI has not arrived and that near-term AGI promises keep being repeated. The normalisation is faithful.

contract.note: Reading 'they' as prominent industry leaders is fair. The contract adds that an earlier deadline must have passed unmet. Musk's 'next year' (2025) did pass, though his outer bound 'within two years' (April 2026) had not by Feb 2026. That is a minor stretch and does not change the result.

evidence.note: ARC Prize, Dec 2025, answers 'Not yet' to whether we have AGI.
Musk, April 2024: AGI 'probably next year, within two years'. An earlier near-term promise; the 2025 date passed.
Musk at Davos, Jan 2026: smarter-than-any-human AI by end of 2026. The promise is repeated with a later date, which implies it had not arrived.

reviews.rationale: A benchmark organisation said in Dec 2025 that AGI had not been reached. Musk's dated statements show the near-term promise made in 2024 and repeated in 2026, with 2025 passing unmet. Only one leader is documented, so 'year after year' rests on thin but adequate evidence.

attribution.note: Marcus's own description of the review in his own post.

semantics.note: Faithful. It keeps both the 'even reasoning-marketed systems' qualifier and the reliance on the Caltech/Stanford review.

contract.note: Fair plain reading. The title variance and the third author's Carleton affiliation are rightly treated as immaterial. 'Latest' is only partly covered because the survey cites many older-model studies.

evidence.note: The review exists and was submitted 5 Feb 2026. Its abstract says significant reasoning failures persist.
The review says reasoning models such as o1-mini remain brittle under simple perturbations.
The review cites tasks that are a significant challenge for state-of-the-art large reasoning models.
The title block lists Caltech and Stanford affiliations (plus Carleton). This confirms the attribution element of the support condition.

reviews.rationale: The review exists, is recent, has Caltech and Stanford authors, and reports significant reasoning failures, including in reasoning-branded and state-of-the-art reasoning models. Coverage of the very latest models is partial, but the claim's substance holds.
